To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the recognition accuracy of a speech recognition system can be significantly increased by exploiting the fact that the acoustic features of a word are not independent, but rather are highly correlated, and 2) the correlation between the acoustic features can be used to estimate the missing feature values.

(1) the recognition accuracy of an ASR system can be improved by using partial information from a spectrographic representation of the acoustic signal, (2) the partial information can be extracted from a cepstral representation of the signal, and (3) this information can be used as a feature vector for the ASR system.

(a) the recognition accuracy of an ASR system is highly correlated with its ability to accurately estimate the acoustic features of the input speech; (b) the acoustic features that are most important to recognition accuracy are those that are the most variable across speakers and environments; (c) these variable acoustic features are those that are most difficult for the ASR system to estimate accurately; and (d) the accuracy with which these features are estimated is strongly influenced by the amount of spectrographic information that is available
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of missing-feature approaches in speech recognition.
the problem of developing new approaches to improving recognition accuracy in difficult acoustical environments, particularly in the presence of noise.
developing missing-feature approaches for ASR that can provide significant improvement in recognition accuracy in the presence of nonstationary and transient disturbances.

missing feature approaches have been very successful in improving the recognition accuracy in noisy environments, especially when the SNR is low.

conventional methods for environmental compensation are effective in improving the performance of speech recognition systems in many important applications today, but there are many important applications in which they are not.

conventional environmental compensation techniques are generally ineffective in coping with the effects of many of the most difficult acoustical conditions that are encountered in many important applications.

we have shown that the conventional approaches for improving speech recognition accuracy in noise are ineffective for many real-world environments and that there are alternative approaches that can provide much greater benefit for many of these more difficult problems.

we are trying to understand the nature of the acoustic variability that affects the accuracy of automatic recognition of speech, to identify the sources of this acoustic variability, and to develop methods to compensate for the effects of this variability on the recognition accuracy.

it is possible to achieve very good speech recognition performance in the presence of noise, reverberation and other distortions by using missing-feature techniques in conjunction with a large vocabulary speech recognition system.

the missing-feature approaches are very effective in improving speech recognition accuracy under a number of adverse conditions.
